content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended that abortion services can be safely provided at the lowest levels of the healthcare system. Training mid-level healthcare providers, such as midwives, nurses, and other non-physician professionals, to perform first-trimester aspiration abortions and manage medical abortions has been proposed as a strategy to improve access to safe abortion care for women. The objective of this study was to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of abortion procedures performed by mid-level providers compared to those performed by doctors. To achieve this, a systematic search was conducted in databases such as CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and POPLINE for studies published between January 1980 and August 15, 2014. Eligible studies included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), prospective cohort studies, and observational studies that compared the safety and/or effectiveness of first-trimester abortion procedures performed by mid-level providers versus doctors. Two independent reviewers screened the abstracts for eligibility and extracted data from the included studies using a standardized form. Meta-analyses were conducted using both fixed-effect and random-effects models to calculate pooled risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Separate analyses were performed based on study design (RCT or cohort) and the type of abortion procedure (medical or surgical). A total of eight studies involving 22,018 participants met the inclusion criteria. Five studies (n = 18,962) assessed surgical abortion procedures, while three studies (n = 3,056) evaluated medical abortion procedures. The surgical abortion studies included one RCT and four cohort studies conducted in the United States, India, South Africa, and Vietnam. The medical abortion studies included two RCTs and one cohort study conducted in India, Sweden, and Nepal. The gestational age limit for surgical abortion was up to 14 weeks, while for medical abortion, it was up to nine weeks. The risk of selection bias was low in the three RCTs, unclear in four observational studies, and high in one observational study. Concealment bias was low in the RCTs but high in all observational studies. None of the studies blinded participants to the type of provider, but this was deemed to have a low risk of performance bias as it was inherent to the intervention. Detection bias was high across all eight studies due to the lack of blinding in outcome assessment. Attrition bias was low in seven studies but high in one study with over 20% attrition. Six studies had unclear risks of selective reporting bias due to unpublished protocols, while two studies had published protocols. Few other sources of bias were identified. For surgical abortion procedures, an analysis of three cohort studies indicated that the risk of abortion failure was significantly higher when performed by mid-level providers compared to doctors (RR 2.25, 95% CI 1.38 to 3.68). However, the quality of evidence for this outcome was rated as very low. There were no significant differences in the risk of complications between mid-level providers and doctors for surgical abortions (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.17 to 5.70 from RCTs; RR 1.38, 95% CI 0.70 to 2.72 from observational studies). When failure and complications were combined, no significant differences were observed between mid-level providers and doctors in both the observational study analysis (RR 1.36, 95% CI 0.86 to 2.14) and the RCT analysis (RR 3.07, 95% CI 0.16 to 59.08). The quality of evidence for these outcomes was considered low for RCTs and very low for observational studies. For medical abortion procedures, there was no significant difference in the risk of failure between mid-level providers and doctors (RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.48 to 1.36 from RCTs; RR 1.09, 95% CI 0.63 to 1.88 from observational studies). The quality of evidence for this outcome was rated as high for RCTs but very low for observational studies. No complications were reported in the three medical abortion studies. In conclusion, there was no statistically significant difference in the risk of failure for medical abortions performed by mid-level providers compared to doctors. Observational data suggest a potentially higher risk of failure for surgical abortions performed by mid-level providers, but the evidence is limited, and more robust data from controlled trials are needed. There were no statistically significant differences in the risk of complications for first-trimester surgical abortions performed by mid-level providers compared to doctors.
